default: It is a month since the ritual: the thirtieth day.

Crestfall is noticeably different. It isn't healed, but it is different. There are six stalls in the market now instead of three. The fountain still isn't running, but somebody has planted bulbs round the foot of it. They are not flowers but onions, which is more honest.

Vorne's garrison is down to eight men, and what they do now looks less like occupying a town than keeping it in repair. The checkpoint on the east road has been moved a mile further out, and two men keep it instead of five.

The Rootless camp has seventeen new people. They came from the villages to the east, having heard that something had changed, and turned towards Crestfall instead of going on east. Maret took them in as briskly as somebody who has been getting ready for exactly this for three years.

default.text: The settlement held for nine days. Then the Compact put up a new curfew without asking anybody, and Maret stopped coming to the meetings.
The settlement held until the Covenant took the grey flag down, and then put it up again the next morning, bigger. Edric says it was not his decision.
The settlement held until a Compact patrol walked through the camp one night. Branch walked them back out to the road. Nobody has called a meeting since.
Somebody goes to look at the seal every month. It is holding, and it is not finished.
The notice nailed to the dry fountain is the Compact's, a timetable for the well in Vorne's hand.
The notice nailed to the dry fountain is the camp's rota for the well, in Branch's square capitals.
One of the three from the gate is Wren. The camp knew him by the second day. He has begun carrying water with the midwife. He hasn't said a word yet, but he carries the water.
One of the three kept at the post is Wren. Nobody there knew him. Aldous went down and told them, and now they let him sit with Wren in the yard for an hour a day.
[missing person] came back on the twenty-ninth day. They read your letter, the honest one, on a bench outside an inn, and then turned round and walked the whole way back.

text.commander:
You and [missing person] have divided the work between you without ever meaning to.

They work with Pol on the account, and with Maret on how the camp is run. You work with Vorne on the Compact's arrangements, and with Edric on the Covenant's new and smaller place.

You find you are seeing to the town's institutions while they see to its people. The two need different things, and each of you has turned out to be right for the half you ended up with.
text.arcane:
The account is finished, and three copies have gone out. What you know is out in the world.

What you had not expected is that now you have time. It is not endless time, and it is not idle time, but it is the time that comes between finishing one piece of work and knowing what the next will be.

On the thirtieth day you go out into Crestfall and try something you haven't done for months. You watch without writing anything down. You look at the market, and the people, and ordinary life coming back into a place that was hurt.

You do it for an hour. At the end of it [missing person] finds you and asks what you were doing.

"Looking," you say.

They nod, as though it were the most ordinary thing you have said in weeks. Perhaps it is.
text.ranger:
The animals have come back further than you can follow from the market square.

You spend the thirtieth day outside the town, in the ordinary forest to the west of Crestfall, reading what the creatures are doing. The forest is coming back in the order these things always go: the animals that can live anywhere first, the ones that need particular things later, and the hunters last of all.

There are no hunters yet. But the creatures they hunt are behaving properly, which means they are expecting hunters to be about, at the right distance. And if they expect hunters, they expect a forest that works as a forest should.

You write it down: the deer expect wolves. You look at it a while. It is the most hopeful thing you have written in a month.
text.cipher:
On the thirtieth day things have settled enough for you to see clearly how they lie.

Vorne will be gone within six weeks. The Compact will keep a token post, two clerks and a line of messengers. It is the best you could have got out of them.

The Rootless camp is recognised, and supplied, and growing. Maret has become the person who matters most to how Ashenveld actually mends, not as a politician but in practice. The camp knows what to do, and it is doing it.

The Covenant is the weakest of the three. Edric is still here, but his people have not come back to him in anything like their old numbers. The Covenant may not keep its hold on Ashenveld now that Seriva has gone and everyone knows what the purification would have cost.

choices.text: Take an honest look. What does Ashenveld still need most?

success.text:
You and [missing person] sit down together and make the list.

Ashenveld still needs time, for the mending to reach the places the curse went deepest. The camp needs a way of carrying on its work that will last. Somebody has to help the people who walked east and have not come back. And there must be a plain account of what happened, for the history of the region.

What Ashenveld doesn't need is another quarrel over who owns the ruins, or any upset while things are changing over, or you going before the change is safe.

The list can be managed. It is the first time in thirty days you have thought so.

success_at_cost.text: You make the list, but some of what is left is beyond you. You write those things down anyway. Things are less overwhelming once they have names.

failure.text:
The list is too long, and you can't find any way of looking at it that makes it manageable. [missing person], watching you struggle with it, takes it away from you.

"What is the most important thing on it?" they ask.

You answer without thinking, and they write it down. "Start there," they say.

text.default:
It is a month since you left Ashenveld.

You are somewhere else altogether. It doesn't matter which town. What matters is that it has nothing to do with ruins, or curses, or factions bargaining over broken mechanisms.

[missing person] has got used to it faster than you. Fourteen months alone in a ruined city have made them, it seems, profoundly grateful for ordinary things. They talk to strangers. They eat everything on the plate. They sleep soundly in strange rooms.

It is you who are still getting used to it.

Ashenveld follows you about, as places do that have changed you. It isn't regret. It has become part of how you look at the world. Wherever you go, you find yourself looking for the signs Ashenveld taught you to look for. Mostly they aren't there. Once or twice they are.

default.text: A letter from Maret catches up with you at an inn. It is three weeks old.
The seal is holding, she writes, but it is not finished. She doesn't ask you to come back. She asks whether you know anybody who can read the old texts.
The garden is green again along the yellow edge, she writes. Lira is teaching a child to tie the knot.

You find them on the fourth day, two towns on, in the back room of an inn, with a fever that broke the night before. They are sitting up. "You came," they say. "You were meant to finish."

"I didn't," you say, and sit down on the end of the bed.

At the inn they last wrote from they tell you that they went on a week ago, thinner than when they came. The innkeeper has a note in their writing: the next town, and the one after, and underneath, "Keep up."

text.commander:
Three weeks out, a letter from Cael reached you. The account has arrived, Vorne is going ahead with the withdrawal, and the Rootless camp has been formally recognised.

You read the letter twice and put it away. The work is going on without you, which is as it should be.

You wonder whether you have finished with that kind of work for good, or whether this is only a gap between one post and the next. You haven't decided. The question will keep.
text.arcane:
The letters from other scholars have begun to arrive, answering the account you sent out. Colleagues at three different places write with questions, and with ideas you hadn't thought of, and with corrections to mistakes you made in a hurry.

It is the ordinary life of a scholar, and it follows you wherever you go.

[missing person] watches you write your replies and says, "Is it strange? Doing this somewhere ordinary?"

"Yes," you say. "But a good strange."
text.ranger:
You are in a town with a market and a forest and birds, and animals behaving in ways you can read without first having to allow for anything poisoning them.

It is a relief, and it is also a kind of grief. You spent weeks learning to read a damaged country, and now there is no need, and you don't know what to do with what you learned.

[missing person], watching you follow a hawk across the market square, says, "You are doing it again."

"Yes," you say.

"It is all right," they say. "I like that you do that."
text.cipher:
Away from the scheming of Ashenveld, you have found that you don't quite know what to want.

In Ashenveld you always knew. You wanted things to go better for the people caught up in it, and the wanting was plain because the situation was plain.

In ordinary life the wanting is less obvious. You are working on it. [missing person], who has been working on it a month longer than you, is sometimes patient with you about it and sometimes not, and you can hardly blame them either way.

choices.text: Think honestly about whether you want to go back to Ashenveld.

default.text:
You think about it for a week.

The answer changes from day to day. Some days it is yes. Ashenveld isn't finished, and you know better than anyone what finishing it would take. Some days it is no. You did what you came to do, and the rest of the work belongs to the people who live there.

By the end of the week you have your answer, and the answer is not yet. That is neither never nor yes, and it is probably the honest place to be.

You tell [missing person]. "I know," they say. They knew before you said it. It seems the ruins teach you to read people very well, and from a distance.

choices.text: Make up your mind. Ashenveld is behind you, and this is what comes next.

default.text:
You decide quickly. A month of hard decisions has made you quicker at them.

Ashenveld was the work, and the work is done. The next work will be something else.

You say so to [missing person]. They look at you for a moment.

"All right," they say. "What next?"

You think about it. You haven't a full answer yet. But at least you are asking the right question.

text.default:
It is the thirtieth day.

You have been in Ashenveld a month, and alone here for a fortnight, since they left.

You won't lie to yourself about it. It is hard. The work isn't; you have the work, and it is good and needed and suits you. What is hard is the evenings, when the work is done and the Tallow is quiet and the fire is lower than it ought to be.

You manage it as you manage most hard things, by doing the next thing. You keep the list up to date. You talk to the people who are here, Maret and Branch and Lira and Pol, and find in those talks something of what an ordinary evening should have in it.

It isn't the same. It will have to do.

On the thirtieth day Joren speaks. He says a whole sentence, in a voice that has not been used for a year, to Pol, who is changing the water by his bed.

"Is there anyone left in Harrow?"

Pol looks at you. Somebody will have to answer him.
text.commander:
Vorne came looking for you last week. He offered you a proper post in the government of the region, as an adviser, with money behind it, doing work that would matter.

You have been thinking about it for seven days. The post would give you a long reach. It would also give you a reason to stay in Ashenveld that would spare you from looking too closely at why staying seems so necessary.

You wonder whether the two can be told apart.
text.arcane:
The work is good. The account is finished and sent out. Pol has become your partner in keeping watch on the curse as it goes back, and you are building a way of keeping that watch that will go on without you if you leave, or with you if you stay.

You are answering the question of whether to stay by keeping both choices open at once. You know that trick. You have used it before. It is what you generally do when you don't want to decide and can't admit it.
text.ranger:
Since the twentieth day Joren has been in the tent by the fire, and every morning you have gone to sit with him.

For a long time he did nothing. Now his hands have stopped being still. They move a little, following the light on the canvas, or the shadows of people going past. Something is coming back.

You don't need him to talk to you. You are glad he is here.
text.cipher:
A fortnight on your own, and you have found something out.

The work is more satisfying when you do it for something you believe in than when you do it for an institution. You believed in Ashenveld getting better before you had any personal stake in it, and losing the personal stake has not changed that.

You are here because the work is here, and you are good at it, and the people here need somebody who is. You find that you don't need a better reason than that.

choices.text: Tell him the truth. There is nobody left.

default.text:
You tell him. He listens with his hands round the bone figure, and nods slowly, as though it were what he expected and needed somebody else to say.

That night he eats for the first time without being asked.

choices.text: Tell him you'll go and look.

default.text: You walk to Harrow and back in two days. The doors are still open, and the tables still laid. You tell him what you saw, all of it, and he asks you to describe one house twice.

choices.text: Be honest with yourself. What do you really need?

success.text:
You sit with the question as the ritual taught you to sit with things, wholly and without putting on any show.

You need the work, and you have it. You need the people you are getting to know here, and you have them. You need to feel you are part of something that matters, and you have that too.

What you are missing is the one who isn't here. You don't pretend you aren't missing them, and you don't try to fill the gap with other things.

You can have most of what you need and still be missing something. There is nothing to be done about that. It is simply how your life is at present.

You look at it honestly, and then you go back to work.

success_at_cost.text:
You get part of the way. You admit what you are missing before you can admit what you have.

Pol, watching you in the herb garden with the look she wears when she is about to say something useful, says, "Onions do not mind being planted in a fountain. They mind not being watered." Then she goes back to her plants, and you are left to work out what she meant.

failure.text:
You can't answer the question today. It isn't a good day for it.

Lira, sitting near by, says without looking up from her rope, "You don't have to know today."

It isn't comfort, exactly. It is permission, and you take it.
